title: Find duplicate elements in an array using HashSet (add each element to set; if `add()` returns false, it is a duplicate).
shortTitle: Find Duplicate Elements in an Array Using HashSet

s1_definition.profdef: A HashSet is a collection that stores only unique elements with average constant time add, contains, and remove. To find duplicates in an array, you iterate once and attempt to add each element to a HashSet. The `add` method returns true if the element was new and false if it was already present, so a false return instantly flags a duplicate. This runs in linear time, O(n), using O(n) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India maintaining a guest list of account numbers that have already entered the vault today. As each person arrives, the guard tries to write their account number on the list. If the number is brand new, it gets written and they pass. If the guard finds the number is already on the list, that is a duplicate entry — someone trying to get in twice — and it is flagged immediately without scanning the whole list by eye.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add each element to a HashSet; if add returns false, you have found a duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A HashSet is a collection that stores only unique elements with average constant time add, contains, and remove. To find duplicates in an array, you iterate once and attempt to add each element to a HashSet. The `add` method returns true if the element was new and false if it was already present, so a false return instantly flags a duplicate. This runs in linear time, O(n), using O(n) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India maintaining a guest list of account numbers that have already entered the vault today. As each person arrives, the guard tries to write their account number on the list. If the number is brand new, it gets written and they pass. If the guard finds the number is already on the list, that is a duplicate entry — someone trying to get in twice — and it is flagged immediately without scanning the whole list by eye.

**One line to remember:** Add each element to a HashSet; if add returns false, you have found a duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
A HashSet is internally backed by a HashMap where the elements are the keys. That is why it offers the same average constant-time operations and why it enforces uniqueness automatically.

The key method is `add`. When you call `seen.add(accountNo)`, it returns true if the element was not already in the set and false if it was. This boolean return is the elegant trick: a false means we have seen this element before, so it is a duplicate. For example `if (!seen.add(accountNo)) duplicates.add(accountNo);` records the account number as a duplicate the moment a repeat is detected. The `contains` method checks membership without adding, as in `if (seen.contains(accountNo))`, and `remove` deletes an element.

Using a set to collect the duplicates themselves, rather than a list, prevents reporting the same duplicate multiple times if an element appears three or more times. If instead you need the count of each duplicate, you would use a frequency HashMap and keep the keys whose count exceeds one.

A senior-level point is the space-time tradeoff. The HashSet approach is linear time but uses extra memory proportional to the number of distinct elements. If memory is tight and you are allowed to modify the input, sorting the array first lets you find duplicates by comparing neighbours with no extra set, but that costs the sort's logarithmic factor in time and destroys the original order. For streaming or very large data, approximate structures like a Bloom filter trade a tiny false-positive rate for drastically less memory. The HashSet method is the standard answer because it is simple, fast, and preserves the input.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a nightly batch file of processed transaction IDs from its payment partner. Due to retries and network glitches, the same transaction ID sometimes appears twice, which would cause double posting to a customer's account like Rajesh's. We must detect any duplicate transaction IDs before posting. This is exactly the duplicate-detection problem, where we add each ID to a HashSet and a failed add reveals a repeat.

Problem 2 — When a duplicate is found, we must report each offending ID exactly once, even if it appears three times, so the operations team can investigate without noise. Collecting the duplicates into another HashSet guarantees each is reported a single time.

In our mini-project we build a `DuplicateDetector` with a `findDuplicates` method that returns the set of transaction IDs that appeared more than once. The demo feeds a batch containing repeats and logs which IDs are duplicates, protecting against double posting.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the transaction IDs TXN-1001, TXN-1002, TXN-1001, TXN-1003, TXN-1002, TXN-1002.

Step 1: We start with an empty seen set and an empty duplicates set. We read TXN-1001. Adding it returns true because it is new, so nothing is flagged.

Step 2: We read TXN-1002. Adding returns true, it is new, nothing flagged.

Step 3: We read TXN-1001 again. Adding returns false because it is already in the seen set, so we record TXN-1001 in the duplicates set.

Step 4: We read TXN-1003. Adding returns true, it is new, nothing flagged.

Step 5: We read TXN-1002 again. Adding returns false, so we record TXN-1002 in the duplicates set.

Step 6: We read TXN-1002 a third time. Adding returns false again, but since duplicates is a set, adding TXN-1002 a second time has no effect, so it is still reported only once.

Step 7: The loop ends. The duplicates set contains TXN-1001 and TXN-1002. Because duplicates were found, the batch is blocked to prevent double posting.

```
[2026-10-26 20:00:02] INFO    Scanned 6 IDs, found 2 duplicate value(s).
[2026-10-26 20:00:02] WARNING Duplicate transaction IDs detected: [TXN-1001, TXN-1002]
[2026-10-26 20:00:02] SEVERE  Blocking batch to prevent double posting.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ids[] = [TXN-1001, TXN-1002, TXN-1001, TXN-1003, TXN-1002, TXN-1002]
    │
    ▼ for each id: seen.add(id)
  TXN-1001 add→true (new)
  TXN-1002 add→true (new)
  TXN-1001 add→false → duplicates += TXN-1001
  TXN-1003 add→true (new)
  TXN-1002 add→false → duplicates += TXN-1002
  TXN-1002 add→false → already in duplicates set (no change)
    │
    ▼
  duplicates = { TXN-1001, TXN-1002 }  → BLOCK batch
```

```
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             DuplicateDetector             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + findDuplicates(ids[]): Set<String>     │  O(n) time, O(n) space
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
      Internals:
        seen: HashSet<String>        (encountered)
        duplicates: LinkedHashSet    (reported once, ordered)
      Contract:
        Pre: ids != null
        Post: returns each repeated value exactly once

  ── State Diagram: Element Status ─────────────────────────

  [NEW add→true] ──seen again──→ [DUPLICATE add→false → record once]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. findDuplicates(ids) → loop seen.add(id)
  2. add→false → duplicates.add(id)
  3. return { TXN-1001, TXN-1002 }
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate elements in an array I use a HashSet, which stores only unique values with average constant-time operations. I iterate once over the array and try to add each element to the set. The add method returns true if the element was new and false if it was already present, so a false return instantly tells me I have found a duplicate. That single boolean is the elegant core of the technique, and the whole algorithm runs in linear time.

A detail I always get right is collecting the duplicates into a second set rather than a list. If an element appears three or more times, a list would record it multiple times and create noise, whereas a set guarantees each duplicate is reported exactly once. When I also need how many times each value repeated, I switch to a frequency HashMap and keep the keys whose count exceeds one.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a settlement de-duplication service. We receive a nightly batch of processed transaction IDs from a payment partner, and because of retries the same ID sometimes appears twice. Posting a duplicate would double-charge a customer like Rajesh, so before posting I scan the batch with a HashSet, and if any duplicate is detected I block the batch and alert the operations team. This simple check directly prevents real financial harm.

The senior-level angle I add is the space-time tradeoff. The HashSet approach is fast and preserves the input order but uses extra memory proportional to the distinct elements. If memory were tight and I could modify the input, I could sort and compare neighbours instead, trading time and the original order for zero extra space, and for massive streaming data I might use a Bloom filter to accept a tiny false-positive rate in exchange for far less memory. For a normal batch, though, the HashSet method is the clean, correct, production choice.
